turns.q: Is Amazon's earnings quality deteriorating? Put operating cash flow beside net income for the last eight quarters, show the accruals ratio trend, tell me whether receivables and inventory are growing faster than revenue over the same windows, and say what that means for the size of our AMZN position.
turns.answer:
Amazon’s earnings quality looks mixed, not clearly broken, but it is softer than it was.
Operating cash flow beside net income over the last eight quarters was $25.28B vs $13.48B, $25.97B vs $15.33B, $45.64B vs $20.00B, $17.02B vs $17.13B, $32.52B vs $18.16B, $35.52B vs $21.19B, $54.46B vs $21.19B, and $26.03B vs $30.25B. That says cash has usually exceeded earnings, but the latest quarter flipped the other way.
The accruals ratio stayed negative, at -3.08%, -10.7%, -10.3%, -9.06%, and -7.56%. The trend has moved up from its trough, which is less favorable than the earlier low, but it is not a collapse.
Receivables are growing faster than revenue over the same window: accounts receivable rose from $50.11B to $75.53B, while revenue rose from $148B to $182B. Inventory is not growing faster than revenue: it moved from $34.11B to $36.53B, while revenue went from $148B to $182B.
For the book, AMZN is $756K and 7.03% of the portfolio, against a portfolio market value of $10.75M. So this is a meaningful position, but not a dominant one. The read argues for caution rather than alarm: earnings quality is not deteriorating in a straight line, but the latest cash-versus-earnings move and the faster receivables build are the two signals that would make me watch the position more closely.

turns.q: How much room does Exxon have if oil falls? Give net debt to EBITDA, EBIT interest coverage and FCF to debt for the latest four quarters against the same four a year earlier, read what the 10-K says about debt maturities and floating-rate exposure, and relate that to our XOM weight and the book's beta to USO.
turns.answer:
Exxon has meaningful balance-sheet room if oil falls, but not unlimited room. On the credit side, the latest four quarters show net debt to EBITDA at -0.29×, -0.38×, -0.25×, and -0.02×. EBIT interest coverage is 96.13×, 61.59×, 48.68×, and 67.91×. FCF to debt is 9209.8%, 817.8%, 619.9%, and 254.0%.
The desk’s comparison read says those same four points are identical a year earlier for all three readings, so there is no year-over-year tightening or loosening in the series shown. The practical read is that Exxon still shows strong interest coverage and positive free-cash-flow support against debt, even though the trend has softened from the very high earlier readings.
The 10-K filing passages on debt maturities and floating-rate exposure were not returned, so I cannot quote them here. The desk also did not return a book beta to USO; only XOM’s beta to USO came back, at 0.33×, which is below 1. That means XOM is materially less sensitive than oil itself, so the portfolio’s downside to an oil fall is cushioned at the name level.
On position sizing, XOM is 4.61% of the portfolio, and Energy is also 4.61%, so XOM is the book’s only Energy exposure in the current composition view. That makes the book’s oil sensitivity essentially the XOM position’s oil sensitivity. Because the book beta to USO was not computable from the run returned, I cannot say whether the whole book is above or below 1.

turns.q: Where does NVIDIA's cash go? Capex, buybacks, dividends and SBC over the trailing twelve months, each as a share of operating cash flow, how each share has moved over three years, and whether the filing states how much buyback authorization remains.
turns.answer:
NVIDIA’s trailing-twelve-month operating cash flow is $134B. Against that, capex is 5.47%, buybacks are 41.2%, dividends paid are 5.01%, and SBC is 5.39%. Buybacks are the dominant cash use by a wide margin.
Over the last three years, capex share rose from 3.81% to 5.05% to 5.88%. Buybacks were much larger throughout, moving from 33.9% to 52.6% before easing to 39.0%. Dividends stayed small, from 1.41% to 1.30% to 0.95%. SBC declined from 12.6% to 7.39% to 6.22%.

turns.q: Is Lilly's margin expansion pricing, mix or cost? Gross, operating and net margin over the last twelve quarters, the gap between gross and operating margin, and what Item 7 attributes the change to. Then compare against Merck, and if Merck is not on the desk, get it ready and tell me what you can say now.
turns.answer:
Lilly’s margin expansion is described by the filing as mainly a gross-margin story, not a pure cost story: “Net income and earnings per share increased in 2025, primarily due to higher gross margin, partially offset by increased marketing, selling, and administrative expenses and research and development expenses.”
On the specific pricing, mix, and cost split, the desk got only a qualitative read, not a full computed decomposition. The filing-language read says 2025 revenue increased primarily by increased volume, partially offset by lower realized prices, while net income rose primarily because gross margin improved. So the evidence points to volume/mix supporting the top line, pricing pressure on revenue, and gross-margin expansion flowing through before overhead and R&D partly absorbed it.
I could not give you the requested quarter-by-quarter margin series for Lilly, because the desk could not settle gross margin, operating margin, or the gross-minus-operating gap from the prepared filing facts. What it did show was net margin for annual points only: 19.7%, 21.9%, 15.4%, 23.5%, and 31.7%. That is not the requested twelve-quarter series.
For Merck, the desk says it is not yet ready on the desk. The quarterly gross, operating, and net margin series were not available, and the gross-minus-operating gap could not be derived. So there is no valid Merck-vs-Lilly comparison yet.
What this means for the book: on Lilly, the current reading is that margin expansion is mostly gross-margin-led with some pricing pressure and some offset from higher selling and R&D spend. On Merck, you do not yet have a like-for-like comparator, so any relative judgment would be premature until the desk returns a typed quarterly panel.

turns.q: Compare the capex intensity and ROIC of Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon over the last three fiscal years. Who spends the most relative to revenue and earns the least on it, and how does that sit with the book's exposure to QQQ?
turns.answer:
On the three-name comparison, Microsoft spends the most relative to revenue at 22.9%, while Amazon earns the least on invested capital at 16.2%. Over the latest fiscal year, capex intensity ranks Microsoft first at 22.9%, Alphabet second at 22.7%, and Amazon third at 18.4%. On ROIC, Microsoft is first at 29.7%, Alphabet second at 24.8%, and Amazon third at 16.2%.
For the last three fiscal years, capex intensity rose for all three names: Microsoft was 13.3%, 18.1%, and 22.9%; Alphabet was 10.5%, 15.0%, and 22.7%; Amazon was 9.17%, 13.0%, and 18.4%.
I cannot tie that to the book’s QQQ exposure, because the desk could not settle a portfolio-level QQQ read for `port_001`. What it did show is that the book holds MSFT at 16.0%, and the analyst said the needed benchmark comparison was unavailable. So the issuer conclusion stands, but the portfolio implication is incomplete: I can say MSFT is the heaviest capex spender and Amazon the weakest ROIC earner in the group, but I cannot say whether that makes the book more or less aligned with QQQ without a visible exposure figure.

turns.answer:
Apple’s working-capital cycle has been negative throughout the period, and it is still negative now. Days sales outstanding rose from 21.43 to 34.89, days inventory moved from 8.74 to 9.45, and days payable increased from 91.05 to 115.40.
The quarter-by-quarter path the desk returned was DSO 21.43, 26.22, 26.09, 28.10, 31.19, 34.89; inventory days 8.74, 11.28, 8.08, 10.79, 12.64, 9.45; payable days 91.05, 93.85, 104.69, 106.72, 119.66, 115.40; and cash conversion cycle -60.87, -56.36, -70.52, -67.83, -75.83, -71.07.
On the three-year range, the latest cash conversion cycle is -71.07, versus a three-year low of -75.83 and a three-year high of -56.36. So the cycle is closer to the low than the high, but it is not at the low.
On supplier financing, the desk did not find a directly quotable latest-10-K passage using that phrase. The latest filing language it retrieved says that "a majority of the Company’s supplier facilities, including manufacturing and assembly sites, are located outside the U.S.", and it discusses supply-chain, receivables, and prepayment risks instead. For the previous 10-K, the desk could not retrieve a separately indexed supplier-financing passage, so it cannot support a quoted wording change between the two filings. It therefore gives you the narrower, supportable answer: the latest 10-K passage retrieved does not discuss "supplier financing" as such, and no filing-quoted comparison to the prior 10-K is available from the record.

turns.q: What share of Amazon's revenue is AWS, how has that share moved over three years, and how much of our AMZN return over the last year relative to SPY does that explain?
turns.answer:
I can’t give you the AWS share or its three-year change from the material I was shown, because the desk’s filing analyst refused the needed figures and only left me quoted context: Amazon says it has three segments, including AWS, and that AWS is separately reported in segment net sales; it also says AWS sales increased 20% in 2025, “primarily reflects increased customer usage,” and that most technology infrastructure assets are allocated to AWS.
On the market side, AMZN’s total return over the last year is -8.12%, SPY’s total return over the last year is 0.00%, so AMZN’s relative return versus SPY over the last year is -8.12%.
What the desk could not do is the key attribution step: it said it cannot attribute a specific portion of that -8.12% to AWS mix changes because it has no method that decomposes stock returns into segment-mix contributions. So the right reading for this book is: AWS is a distinct and growing part of Amazon’s business, but the desk cannot support a quantified claim that AWS mix drove the one-year underperformance versus SPY.
